extracted.intended_audience: education researchers, program evaluators, and K–12 assessment designers
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, administering, and scoring grade-5 student essays using a combination of a holistic rubric (adapted from the College Board SAT guide) and six analytic trait rubrics from the 6+1 Trait Writing model, plus teacher-survey fidelity measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a consistent prompt
rubrics_metrics.description: The prompt used for the study was the same for both the pretest and the posttest: "Think of a skill you have learned that has made your life easier or more fun. Write a letter telling about your skill, explain how you learned it, and why you think it is important."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of the same prompt throughout the study was intended to avoid variation in student performance that could be related to the characteristics of different writing modes (for example, explanatory writing versus persuasive writing) or specific prompts. Rather than narrowly specifying what must be explained in the essays, students were allowed to choose what they wished to explain, within the general guideline provided by the prompt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test administration: three-day writing process and proctoring rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Students completed planning, drafting, revising, and a final version over three class periods of about 45 minutes each on three consecutive or near-consecutive school days. Teachers proctored sessions and followed explicit directions and verbatim scripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dictionaries and thesauruses were allowed; the use of spelling or grammar checkers was not. Students were to work on their own, without assistance from peers or teachers. All student essay booklets were kept by the teacher between class sessions; students were not allowed to work on them at home or during other parts of the school day. Teachers were instructed not to give any assistance to students beyond the information provided in the verbal instructions. Test administration directions specified how each of the three class periods should be structured and how the process should be explained to students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blinding and mixing procedures to prevent scoring bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Pretest and posttest essays (and essays from treatment and control schools) were mixed together and delivered to raters at the same time; raters were blind to whether an essay was pretest/posttest or treatment/control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesapeake Research Associates relabeled student essays with coded identification numbers and sent them to the essay rating team. Essays were photocopied, labeled with new unique identification numbers, and shipped so that raters—and the REL Northwest research team—were blind to the source of the essays during scoring. After scoring, original identifiers were restored for analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic scoring rubric (adapted from College Board SAT guide)
rubrics_metrics.description: A slightly modified version of a scoring guide used for college entrance examinations (derived from the College Board 2005 SAT writing scoring guide) produced a single overall writing-quality score for each essay. Scores ranged from 1 to 6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One phrase within one item on the scoring guide was altered because it was oriented specifically toward scoring a persuasive rather than an expository essay. Student scores resulting from application of the holistic rubric were used as the primary outcome variable for the study. For both holistic and trait scores, raters assigned 1 (severely flawed; very little or no mastery) to 6 (clear and consistent mastery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic trait rubrics: six core traits (6+1 Trait Writing model)
rubrics_metrics.description: A second scoring team applied six separate rubrics, one for each of the six core traits in the 6+1 Trait Writing model (the trait of presentation was not scored).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These trait-specific scores were included as additional outcome measures because their alignment with the intervention might result in more sensitivity to program effects. The six trait scales were positively correlated with the holistic scale and together accounted for a large portion of variance in the holistic score. (The report notes that presentation was not scored because students did not have the opportunity to address presentation issues during the assessment—the test booklet required a standard presentation format.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Rater scoring procedure and discrepancy resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Each student essay was scored independently by two raters. Each rater assigned a 1–6 score; the final score was the average of the two, scored in half-point increments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the two raters' scores were identical or only one point apart, no further action was taken. If the two scores were more than one point apart, the essay was flagged and scored by the team leader, who then asked the two original raters to read the essay again and revise their scores in consultation with her. This procedure was used both as quality assurance and for continual improvement of the rating team.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of unscorable or ineligible essays
rubrics_metrics.description: Pretests that were blank, illegible, written in a language other than English, or deemed 'too short to score' were assigned the lowest possible score. Essays not in English and essays of two sentences or less were coded as 'unable to rate' and assigned the lowest possible score during analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all students who completed the pretest received a pretest score; specific exclusion reasons were recorded and those records were assigned the lowest score prior to data analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility rules for including students in analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Student eligibility to participate in the study was established retrospectively using demographic information supplied by schools. Students not in grade 5 and students eligible for 'modifications' on statewide assessment were removed; students eligible for 'accommodations' were included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These eligibility criteria were established before any data collection occurred. Examples: 99 multigrade students not in grade 5 were removed; 22 students eligible for 'modifications' were removed; students with accommodations (minor alterations in test-taking procedures) remained in the sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imputation of missing posttest scores
rubrics_metrics.description: For students who did not complete a posttest but did complete a pretest, posttest scores were statistically imputed based on other data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final analytic sample included all eligible-to-participate students who completed pretest and posttest; in addition, imputation methods were applied for missing posttests to retain students with pretests in the analysis. Sensitivity analyses were performed to evaluate robustness of findings to modeling choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher-survey fidelity instrument: scales and scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: A teacher survey included 10 scales corresponding to the 10 classroom practices emphasized by the intervention; each scale contained 3–7 items rated on a seven-point scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale scores were created by taking the mean of items within each scale for each teacher. The survey was administered at baseline, midyear, and end-of-year. At initial administration, internal consistency of scales ranged from 0.78 to 0.92. The survey was intended to measure the degree to which teachers implemented the practices promoted in the intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision not to score presentation trait
rubrics_metrics.description: The presentation trait from the 6+1 model was not scored because students did not have the opportunity to address presentation issues during the assessment—the test booklet required that they use a standard presentation format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an assessment format constrains a particular dimension of writing (here, presentation), that trait may be excluded from scoring to avoid measuring something students could not reasonably demonstrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures to maintain data linkage and student privacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Student essay booklets and classroom rosters used prerecorded unique student identification numbers structured so researchers could determine district, school, and classroom while preventing access to student names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two copies of each roster were maintained at the school; at the end of data collection, a copy was made for the research team with the column of student names removed. Identifiable information about individual students was never transferred from the districts to the researchers; parental consent and student assent were not required given the non-transfer of identifiable data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality assurance through rater experience and pooling
rubrics_metrics.description: The rating team consisted of experienced raters who have scored papers for school districts and other clients for decades and are experienced with trait-based and holistic rubrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each essay was scored by two teams: one applied the holistic rubric and a second applied the six analytic rubrics. Use of experienced raters and the two-team approach, combined with blinding and discrepancy-resolution procedures, formed the study's quality assurance for outcome measurement.
